speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 61, to give effect to a convention for the unification of certain rules relating to international carriage by air, to make provision for applying the rules contained in the said convention, subject to exceptions, adaptations and modifications, to carriage by air which is not international carriage within the meaning of the convention, and for purposes connected therewith.

subtopic: BILL TO GIVE EFFECT TO WARSAW CONVENTION OF OCTOBER 12, 1929
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: BILL TO GIVE EFFECT TO WARSAW CONVENTION OF OCTOBER 12, 1929
speechtext: The purpose of this bill is to give effect to the convention adopted at Warsaw, in 1929 to unify the rules for international carriage of goods and passengers by air. This convention has been adopted by Great Britain, Ireland, the United States, Mexico and practically all European countries. In view of the increase in international carriage by air it is felt that Canada should ratify this convention. The bill provides that in addition to governing international carriage by air the provisions of the Warsaw convention can by order in council be applied to carriage by air within Canada. The bill also provides for limitation of liability for loss of passengers and baggage.

speechtext:
1.	How many Canadian nationals of German extraction in December, January and February, last, asked for passports to visit Germany or to go through other European countries to go to Germany?

2.	What is the purpose of their visits abroad?
3.	Will the government enforce the Foreign Enlistment Act if these are going to enlist in Germany or for German aggression?
4.	Will any amendments be made to existing statute law to prevent these migrants ever returning to Canada in the future at any time?
5.	Has Canada recognized or been asked to recognize the illegal conquest by force by Germany of Czecho-Slovakia, Austria, the Rhine, Hungary and other nearby nations contrary to international law and treaties?
6.	Will any correspondence in relation thereto be tabled ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONALS IN GERMANY-QUESTION OF RECOGNITION OF GERMAN CONQUESTS
speechtext:
1.	In the months of December, January and February, last, 72 Canadian nationals, apparently of German extraction, were accorded passport facilities for visits abroad, including Germany. Of these 72 Canadians, 41 were men, 17 women and 14 children. Of the 41 men, 7 were under the age of 30.
2.	In all but two cases the purpose of the journey was stated to be "making a visit." One applicant stated that he desired to reside permanently and another that he was travelling on business.
3.	There is no indication that the hypothetical case set forth in the question has arisen. If it had arisen, the Foreign Enlistment Act would not be applicable, in the present situation.
4.	No occasion has arisen for legislative action and no amendments to existing statute law's are in contemplation. If an occasion arose, it could be adequately dealt with under existing legislation.
5.	As regards Austria, there has been de facto recognition of German sovereignty, on the part of Canada as of other countries. No action has been taken as regards Czechoslovakia.
No information has been received with regard to the conquest by Germany of the Rhine or of Hungary.
6.	It is not the present intention to table correspondence in relation to these matters.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION-DISCUSSION ON EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EASTER RECESS
speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader
of the opposition (Mr. Manion) asked me last week if I would indicate to the house what further legislation would likely be brought down during the present session. I intimated to my hon. friend that I would endeavour to do so to-day.
Hon. members will have noticed that since the question was addressed to the government a number of measures have been added to the order paper, and on the order paper of to-day, under introduction of bills and government orders, will be found most of the legislation remaining to be dealt with at the present session. So far as I have been able to ascertain, the following are the only additional bills likely to be introduced:
Bills respecting: Live stock and live stock products; cheese and cheese factory improvement; agricultural products cooperative marketing; cattle and beef marketing.
A possible amendment to the Dairy Industry Act.
A bill providing for the constitution of a salt fish board.
Two minor amendments to the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
A bill respecting official secrets.
A bill making provision for the sealing of royal instruments.
Certain amendments to the criminal code.
Probably a bill concerning the office of Chief Justice of Canada.
Possible amendments to the National Revenue Act.
A bill respecting the Toronto harbour commissioners.
[Mr. Church.}
A bill to give effect to the provisions of a convention with the United States providing for emergency regulations of the level of Rainy lake and other boundary waters.
A government bill respecting interest on small loans will be introduced in the senate. Other measures from the Department of Finance include a bill to create a mortgage rediscount bank, a Canadian National railway financing and guarantee bill, and a bill to amend the Gold Clause Act.
It is necessary to mention, in addition, possible legislation in the nature of amendments to existing acts arising out of the budget; possible minor amendments to some other existing acts, and such legislation as may arise out of the recommendations of special standing committees. There are also the supplementary estimates.
I think that gives the program very completely. Something may arise of which I have not knowledge at the moment, but so far as I have been able to ascertain, the house now has before it the legislative program for the remainder of the session.
Hon. R. .T. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :	The program certainly seems a
fairly liberal one, using the word not in its political sense. I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman if he will state what day is likely to be set aside for the discussion of the international crises through which we have passed since last September. A week or two ago I believe the right hon. gentleman told one of the members from Toronto, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), that he would deal with the matter shortly, and I should be glad if he would inform the house when he is likely to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I thought one statement

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In 1938 our total imports of raw cotton, not further manufactured than ginned, were valued at $17,400,000, in round figures. Of that amount $58,000 worth came from the United Kingdom, $16,900,000 worth from the United States, $378,000 worth from Egypt and $42,000 worth from British India. Also under this item we imported cotton linters, not further manufactured than ginned, to a total value of $414,000. of which $395,000 worth came from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The observations I wish to make at this time are somewhat similar to those which have been made. In this instance they apply more particularly to the excise tax, and to loss of revenue which will result to Canada from the passing of the legislation We will relieve the Canadian importer from paying the three per cent excise tax on imports valued at $16,900,000. In other words, Canada has made a trade gift of a half a million dollars on this particular item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To whom?

Both ways, but much more so to the impoverishment of the Canadian treasury. In charge of that treasury at the present time is an administration following in the footsteps of the Fielding Liberals, who for years enunciated in the house the doctrine of revenue taxation with which to run the country. To my mind this half million dollars on cotton could be considered a tax of a kind which would meet with the approval of the Fielding Liberals, who believed they must have revenue from taxation of this kind rather than give tariff protection. I admit there is an element of protection in that three per cent, and I admit what is in the mind of the minister right now, that cotton goods might eventually cost the Canadian consumer a little less-but not a great deal.
As to the other question I had in mind, I doubt very much whether I shall receive an answer to it. I say that because now we have the spectacle of the Minister of Trade and Commerce handling the section of the treaty which has to do with the concessions the United States have given us-I use the word "concessions" because the Prime Minister used it. The Minister of Finance has to answer for the so-called concessions we have given to the United States. Even though the dollar value in straight duty concessions is two to one against us, when we come to consider the free items we find that then will be far less revenue to the dominion treasury after the excise tax provision is done away with. I have studied the many answers

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
which have been given, but still I cannot see what concessions Canada has received to offset the eventual removal of the three per cent excise tax in respect of these free items. I do not know what we are going to get back for the half million dollars we are giving with this particular concession. I know what the minister's answer will be, but I want to discharge my responsibility and to go on record as saying that this is a departure from the tariff-for-revenue policy, which was part and parcel of the 1919 platform of the Liberal party. It will make it more difficult for those who follow the Minister of Finance in years to come to balance the budget. I do not know of any provision which has been made to balance the equation with Egypt on the one hand and to assist the British empire trade from India on the other. To my mind the three per cent narrowed the preference with British India, which is really an evasion of the spirit of the 1932 trade agreement. This is another one of the trade gifts from the treasury of Canada which in the aggregate will amount to a million dollars a month.

Two or three years ago a royal commission inquired into the textile

I submit that I speak for a large number of people who have to buy textiles. He cannot buy them if he has no money in his pocket.

These are matters of concern to the people of Canada. There are those of us who feel that this industry has extracted large sums of money from the people by way of increased prices under a protective tariff. I do not want to discuss this matter at length, but I wish to protest, on behalf of the people whom I represent in this parliament.

Hon. members rise to discuss textiles generally, but they forget that there are many kinds of textiles. For instance, there are woollen textiles, worsted textiles, cotton textiles, rayon textiles and many other types. Because certain things were brought

out by the Turgeon commission there has been a general condemnation of the textile industry. If hon. members will examine the financial statements of the woollen textile industry they will find that many of the claims made against that industry on the floor of this house have been absolutely without foundation. The fact of the matter is that during the worst years of the depression the woollen textile industry proved to be the greatest boon in the matter of employment. In spite of the protection they received, the products of this industry were purchased by the consumer of Canada at a lower price than they had in twenty-five years, a condition which was brought about by internal competition in the industry. I should like to add a word to what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has just said. The imports under this particular item of wearing apparel made from vegetable fibres were, in 1935, $254,000, and that increased in the year just closed, 1937, to $396,000. Taking the preceding item, the imports of cotton clothing and cotton textile manufactures increased from $589,000 in 1935 to $980,000 in 1937; imports of fabrics wholly of cotton increased from $520,000, in 1935, to $992,000 in 1937; imports of woven fabrics wholly of cotton, bleached or mercerized, increased from $889,000, in 1935, to $1,438,000 in 1937; and the imports under item ex 523, woven fabrics wholly of cotton, not bleached, increased from $512,000, in 1935, to $1,341,000 in 1937. That is to say, the imports under each item almost doubled since 1935. ,
My reason for rising at this time is again to point out that this is an industry which was reestablished at the so-called Bennett emergency session of parliament, and the return brought down by the national employment commission reflects the effects in increased employment of the measure of protection embodied in that legislation. If one looks at the returns of the national employment commission and takes into consideration the average increase of population, which since 1929 has been 9-96 per cent, one observes that there is an increase of 11,234 people employed in the textile industry
over the number employed previously to the implementing of the legislation which was passed at that emergency session.

That many more people
are employed in factories?

Yes, in textile factories. I am taking the figures in the Purvis report under the heading of Fibres, Textiles and Their Products. When you consider the increase in population, which is taken on a basis of ten per cent in ten years, you find that there are 11,234 more people working in the textile industry to-day than were employed in that industry prior to the enactment of the 1930 legislation.
Of all the things Canada needs at the present time it is that we should all get together, entirely apart from political considerations, and see if we cannot get our people back to work. Here is an outstanding example of an industry in which close to 12,000 more of our Canadian people are being employed. I have every sympathy with the consumer in the cost of this material. I know the consumer is very much concerned. Any one of us, if forced to do it, could make observations from the point of view taken by my hon. friend who has just left the chamber; but should we not, Mr. Chairman, have as our first consideration the fact that a great number of our people in Canada are now unemployed, that 157,000 are now looking for jobs? Twenty thousand have been taken care of by primary industry in its expansion, I will admit; but there has been a shrinkage of 157,000 in the number of people engaged in secondary industry. Here is one of the very few majoi secondary industries in this country in which there has been a substantial improvement in employment since 1930.
Then we come to the 1935 agreement, and we see an increase in the importations, which, I think the Minister of Finance will agree, have practically doubled in the last three years, the real reason being the 1935 agreement. Now we have consummated another trade agreement which went into effect on January 1, 1939, and if we add the cumulative effects of the last three years to what is going to take place in the next three, it is difficult to come to the conclusion that there will be any real expansion of employment in this country. My main point is that these three very important departments, labour, commerce and finance, do not seem to be characterized by any cohesion or cooperation or correlation with respect to unemployment. In spite of the Turgeon report and the free trade philosophy

First, however, I should like to make some reference to what has been referred to already, the action that was taken in setting up what is known as the Turgeon commission to investigate the textile industry.
This commission went into a good many of our towns and investigated a number of our textile concerns. Unfortunately, while I believe it was set up as a fact finding commission, at times the attitude of commission counsel was such as to approach what might be called persecution in regard to these different industries.

That was undoubtedly true; the smaller concerns engaged in the manufacture of knitted goods and socks and stockings certainly increased their business to a considerable extent. I should like to point out just what has been done in connection with the knitted goods schedules and the socks and stockings items. When the Turgeon commission was sitting in a small town in Ontario the editor of the local newspaper asked permission to make a statement at the close of the hearing. His request was acceded to, and he went on to tell what the two small textile industries located in that town had done for it. He said these industries were founded in 1903, when the town had a population of some two thousand. Since then, coincident with the growth of these industries, the town had developed and progressed until at the time of the hearing its population had doubled. He quoted figures showing that the employees of the textile industries of that town paid over twenty-five per cent of the total taxes, and that less than one-fifth of one per cent of the unpaid taxes was owed 'by these employees. He stated further that the debenture debt of the town had been cut in two during the worst years of the depression, and said that was directly attributable to the payrolls of these companies. He also stated that during the thirty-three years these companies had been operating they had never been convicted under the minimum wage act and that the wage earners of the town had never suggested that a labour union should be organized. I should like to quote the final words of his statement as they appear in the report of the commission:
The receipt of steady incomes by the mill employees and their consequent ability to pay their taxes, water and hydro bills, has been the main factor that has made possible our miles of street and sidewalk paving, our fire protection, hydro, water works and sewer systems, and the upkeep of our hospitals, schools, churches, public library and many other byroads of life that spell comfort, convenience and social development-all unsurpassed in any town of our size in Canada. The district benefits too because the products it grows are sold in town to the mill employees, so the fabric of prosperity is so intertwined that we are all interdependent on one another. The heads of the company are leaders in all the town's philanthropies, and one fact is also certain, that to an unusual degree there are on the company payroll employees who because of age and infirmity would not be on the average payroll in mills elsewhere-and are only on there because of the kindly heart of the men at the top. We whose experience goes back many years, who have seen our town march hand in hand with the company, step by step up the ladder that has brought us to our present position I know would deplore as a tragedy any drastic change that would result in lower-mg our standard of living, because without our mills there would soon be moss growing on our streets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whose submission is it?

The recommendation made as to how this can be accomplished-
That is, the solution of the coal problem.
-is that all importations of coal should be forthwith taken under the control of the dominion government by legislation, and that all future importations of American coal should be made under government permit. Approximately 1,000,000 tons of Canadian coal go into the United States annually as against over 14,000,000 tons imported from the States last year. As a matter of permanent policy the States might be given permits to send into Canada ton for ton against what they take from us. As regards all further importations of American coal, they should come in under a quota to be fixed annually, such quota getting less each year as the market adapted itself to Canadian coal and supplies became available, until eventually the Canadian market was reserved exclusively for Canadian coal. The Dominion Fuel Board might well be given extended powers and be asked to assist in working out the policy indicated.
If the carrying out of this policy were spread over a short period of years, eastern industries and eastern householders would be able gradually to adapt themselves to the use of Canadian coal as replacements in equipment were made, and as they gradually became accustomed to the best methods of burning Canadian coal. . . .
In negotiations with our friends across the border, no objection in principle can be taken to the permit and quota system above suggested. It has been put in force by the American government in relation to Canadian cattle going into the States. It has been put in force by Britain in reference to the acceptance of Canadian bacon and other agricultural products. It is not subject to the same objections, during the pending trade negotiations, that would be urged against any increase in existing tariffs. Coal is actually to-day the subject of an agreement permitting the entry into the Irish Free State of British coal, in exchange for permission to send Irish cattle into the British markets. This agreement has been renewed recently, showing the satisfactory results secured by both parties under the original agreement.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I intend to support the bill as far as it goes because I believe that the pension appeal court has outlived its usefulness. It has discredited itself in the eyes of all returned men's organizations and probably in the eyes of all those people who are familiar with the administration of the Pension Act.
I should like to associate myself with the remarks of previous speakers in asking that the bill be referred to a special committee to investigate certain problems of major importance that are confronting pensioners.

Pension Act Amendment
I intend to deal only with what I consider one of the main problems facing pensioners, namely, the case of the non-pension widow. To-day there are very few people in Canada who realize that when a married pensioner dies, his pension dies with him automatically unless his wife is in the fortunate position of being able to prove to a somewhat hard-boiled medical board that his death was on account of war service, or unless he was receiving an eighty per cent pension; and of course, many years after the close of the war, it is not such an easy matter to prove that death is on account of war service.
To-day we are living in a time of wars and rumours of war, and I suggest that it is high time the government took steps to acknowledge in full the country's obligations to its pensioners. I do not believe that those obligations are being met in full to-day. Should Canada become involved in another war, I know, speaking for myself, if I were told that in the event of my being seriously wounded and, at a later date, dying after the war, my wife would not receive my pension, I would not consider that my country was dealing in an honourable manner with my widow. Any country that would expect men to be willing to sacrifice their lives for it, without unconditionally accepting full responsibility for the care of those men's dependents, is a country in which there is something radically wrong.
I believe the majority of the members of this house have on their files cases of widows who to-day are suffering from a great injustice. I shall refer briefly to one case with which I am familiar. It illustrates very well the injustice that widows are suffering from today. The case is that of a healthy man, a great football player, who enlisted and had his leg blown off. It was amputated at the thigh and he had to undergo several additional operations, which left the stump of the leg in a very sore state so that he was unable to wear an artificial limb. Eventually the weight of his body broke down his other foot so that he could not take proper exercise. Internal diseases followed and finally he died in 1933. Two doctors who attended him both gave evidence that his death was the result of war service. An application for a pension was turned down by the pension board and an appeal was taken to the appeal court. That also was turned down. In 1936 the case was referred to me and I got in touch with the veterans' bureau. We succeeded in getting Doctor Laidlaw, a well-known pathologist in Canada, to take an interest in the case. He submitted evidence to the effect that undoubtedly the man's death was the result of war service. On that evidence we got the appeal court to reopen the case. It was again referred to the pension board, and again a pension was refused.
In the middle of 1938, for some reason or another, somebody, the government or the pension board, had a change of heart and, without a change in the act, that woman was awarded a pension, five years after the death of her husband. In other words, the country had deprived her of her rightful pension for five years. She had been robbed of approximately $3,000 by the government's not acknowledging the fact that a pension was due her. The pension was not made retroactive; that is not possible under the law. There are many similar cases in Canada to-day, and therefore I say that we are not meeting our obligations to the dependents of returned men.
Before the committee that sat in 1936 it was made perfectly clear on many occasions that it was not so much a matter of what a pensioner was entitled to as of what the country could afford to pay. In other words, the country was in a bankrupt state, paying only so many cents on the dollar of its obligation. It was stated in this house by one of its leaders that Canada had been very generous to its returned men. I suggest that when a debtor pays his creditor he is not being generous; he is merely meeting his obligations, and when he does not pay his debt in full he does not meet his obligations. That is the state of Canada to-day in relation to this question. Canada is not meeting its obligations to the dependents of the returned men. To-day, twenty years after the war, we find that we still have many obligations which are left undischarged so far as our returned men are concerned. I therefore add my voice to those of other hon. members in asking that the bill be referred to a special committee to investigate some of the major problems confronting pensioners [DOT] at the present time.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
There are two important changes in this bill, and while most hon. members would like to see the minister bring down a bill with many more changes going further, still it is only fair to say the two changes that are proposed will, in my opinion at any rate, bring about some measure of relief to the returned men. I refer to the change in connection with the appeal court and the extension of time for applications.
In 1936 when the committee met it was proposed to do away with the appeal court; but it seems that the country was not quite
Pension Act Amendment

ready for that move because, although the agitation has been kept up since that time, it is only now that legislation is introduced to do away with the appeal court. I agree with a good deal that has already been said, but I disagree with some of the speakers who are advocating that this bill go before a committee. I had the honour of being on the last committee, and I think I can say correctly that almost every aspect, yes, every aspect, of the returned men's problems was dealt with during the time that committee sat in 1936. Those problems may have become aggravated since that time, but to my mind they are essentially the same as they were then. They may be greater, but they are the same. It seems to me that after the deliberations of that committee and, later, the exhaustive research made by the veterans' assistance commission, the minister and hon. members are very well seized of most if not all of the problems confronting the returned men. I doubt whether there is one phase of the whole soldier problem that cannot be discussed on the floor of the house, either before the bill goes into committee or when it is in committee.
I wish to add my meed of praise to what has been said with respect to the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power). I think I can say without fear of successful contradiction that he is, if not the most sympathetic, one of the most sympathetic ministers we have had in this house in charge of returned men's problems. No one knows the problems of the returned men better than he does, and I have no apologies to offer for voicing my word of praise of the minister.
I know that we should not at this stage discuss the various clauses of the bill, but I want to speak of one aspect, that of doing away with the appeal court. I believe that some further changes will have to be made, because I find that some aspects of the new set-up would appear to preclude many applicants from getting redress to which I think they are entitled. I have one case before me which is very interesting and might be cited in support of what I have to say as to the need for additional phraseology in the bill to provide that special cases may be given attention. This man, Mr. Gibbs, enlisted in 1916 and served until 1919 in Prance with notably meritorious service. He took ill in 1919 and died in 1921. The doctor who attended him gave it as his considered opinion that this man died from cancer, something he contracted while he was in the army. His widow at the time did not make claim because there was some insurance money coming; but in course of time, after the insurance money had
[Mr. Reid.l
been spent, she appealed to the board of pension commissioners or the tribunal for a pension, and they granted her one. An appeal, however, was taken against the award, and the appeal court reversed the finding and refused pension to the widow.
The strange feature is that the appeal court stated that the whole matter hinged on medical evidence, yet they themselves reversed the award on lay evidence. By that I mean that in 1921 the widow said she noticed this growth on her husband's neck in 1920; then in 1933, when the appeal was up, she said it was 1919 when she noticed the growth. But the sad part is that although the court of appeal stated that the matter hinged on medical evidence, the medical practitioner who gave evidence in the case stated it as his unqualified opinion that the man died as a result of cancer he contracted and had in his body when he returned from overseas. I doubt whether the present bill would touch cases of that kind, unless some proviso is made that a case may be reopened without additional evidence being produced. No new or additional evidence can be produced in a case of that kind, so, without some further provision, this woman will be denied a pension to which I feel she is entitled.
I was pleased when the Minister of Pensions provided hospitalization for non-pensioners. That has been a great advantage, but I should like to see it go a little further. It seems hardly fair that those receiving $20 or $40 a month under war veterans' allowance should have moneys deducted from their allowance during the time they are in hospital. I do not see why they should be called upon to pay, while others receive the benefit freely, and rightly so, of course, if they come under the new regulations.
In passing, I should like to draw the minister's attention to the condition of Shaugh-nessy hospital in Vancouver. The building was built in 1909 and was used as a school before being taken over by the military authorities. I am not going to say it is a fire-trap, but it is old and was never adapted for a military hospital. With the change in regulations there is no doubt there will be additional demand for hospital accommodation in Vancouver for many years to come, and I would ask the minister to give this matter his serious consideration. I understand plans were drawn up for a new building many years ago, but nothing further was done about the matter.
If protests do come mostly from hon. members representing British Columbia, it is hardly to be wondered at, because British Columbia

Pension Act Amendment
has a greater proportion, of returned men in proportion to population, either pensioners or those receiving war veterans' allowance, than any other province. Just before coming to the house to-night I noted some statistics concerning this. I find that in Ontario there are 5,135 in receipt of war veterans' allowance; in British Columbia, 3,512; in Quebec, 1,476; in Manitoba, 1,372; in Alberta, 1,131; in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, 766; in Saskatchewan, 807; and in New Brunswick, 390. So it appears that British Columbia has twenty-seven per cent of the total number in receipt of war veterans' allowances. The same condition applies as to pensions. Out of 79,864 pensioners, Ontario has 27,549; British Columbia, 10,643; Quebec, 5.499; Manitoba, 7,377; Alberta, 5,821; Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, 4,523; Saskatchewan, 4,306; and New Brunswick, 2.162. Those figures I believe prove what I say, that British Columbia is carrying a heavier load, because disabled ex-service men are there in greater numbers. In further support of this statement, the figures given to the minister by the veterans' assistance commission show that when they were proposing economic allowances, which we are still advocating, they gave a total of 4,650 who would be in receipt of such allowances in Ontario, while in British Columbia they estimated the total would be 6,354. When one compares the population of Ontario, almost 3,000,000, with the population of British Columbia, something over 700,000, one realizes that in British Columbia, the problem is greater and more difficult than in any other province. That is why the voice of British Columbia is heard perhaps more vociferously, through its members in this house and the provincial legion organizations, than is the case with other provinces.
Nearly everv speaker has said something regarding the plight of the widows, which hon. members must realize is very serious, and which condition demands that something be done for them. Take the case of a returned man in receipt of a pension of, say $7.50 or $15 a month, with the man and his wife endeavouring to carry on as best they may on this meagre amount. Suddenly the man passes away; the pension is cut off, and how is the widow to carry on for the rest of her days? Heaven only knows. Surely there is some responsibility on this house and this government in regard to these widows, and the plight of ex-service men on relief is even worse. I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to their plight.
I think something should be said with regard to the loyalty of the returned men during
these days of stress. I know some people have laughed at the latest move of the returned men's organizations in proposing to organize in defence of Canada; but to me at least it shows that they are still loyal to Canada, and in my opinion that loyalty is well worth preserving. I may have something further to say when the bill is in committee, but I felt that I should at least say this much, particularly on behalf of the widows and before the bill reaches the committee stage.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several times in this house I have spoken briefly in support of greater consideration for our returned soldiers. It is my opinion, in which I am becoming more confirmed each year, that Canada is not playing fair with the returned men. I think we are forgetful of the fact that each year our returned men and their wives are getting one year older and consequently one year weaker. I do not think we heed the fact that each year there are actually fewer jobs available in this country. We doctor up our statistics in order to make a rather pleasant appearance on paper, but there is no pleasant appearance to be found when we walk the streets of any of our large cities. Each year we see more young people coming into the labour market to take what jobs are available, and each year it becomes more difficult for a man over forty to obtain a position of any kind. In addition, each year there are fewer markets for the commodities people used to produce and by means of which they were enabled to get by. I recall that twelve years ago, we will say, a person could go into any ordinary little community and milk a few cows, plant a good garden, raise a few strawberries, make butter and so on, and find a sufficient market for those commodities to enable him to get by. Then again, in almost every little community it was possible for people to maintain themselves 'by knitting, sewing, making clothes, doing washings and things of that kind. Many of the widows of fifteen years ago, with the help of their children, were able to carry on in this way; but, sir, to-day it is becoming increasingly difficult to secure a livelihood through these avenues. There is a little dairy, a little milk distributing establishment, in every small town to-day, with someone making a business of it, where fifteen years ago there was no such thing.
I believe we must take cognizance of these matters, for they have an important bearing on this whole question of our returned men and their dependents, especially their widows. I am going to suggest what may seem a little radical, but what I think is only justice. The
Pension Act Amendment

recommendation of the veterans' assistance commission, which was couched in the following words, should be implemented at once, that-
-unemployed indigent veterans with service in a theatre of actual war be taken care of by the dominion government while unemployed, and paid unemployment assistance accordingly.
So far as I know, that recommendation has not yet been implemented; I think it should be attended to without further delay. War widows should receive an allowance forthwith, for the reasons I have already indicated. During the last month I have spoken with at least a dozen war widows who have sat down beside me and in blunt sincerity asked, "What can I do to make a living?" It would challenge the best intelligence of this house to tell them what should be done. Certainly I could not tell them, but those widows had to make a living and they had to educate their children.
I think it is time we laid down the principle that all men who saw service in an actual theatre of war should receive $40 a month, and that on their death their widows should receive the same amount without any questions asked. People may say, "Well, where is the money coming from?" It is not my business to discuss that; probably I would be called to order if I did; but without discussing it at all I am going to point out this fact, that thirty years from to-day everyone will be able to see where the money could have come from, and everyone will wonder what kind of dolts we were that we could not see it also. There is no question about that at all. If a war were to break out within the next two or three days, we would be finding money in abundance in order to kill men. It is high time we found money in abundance in order to save men. Just while I am on that point, if I may digress for a moment, I think it is clearly recognized by all who are prepared to face the facts that it would be impossible for this country to engage in a war of the dimensions of the last war and go into debt for the money necessary to conduct such a war. We would have a structure of debt under which we would be absolutely crushed. Clearly, if war came, a way would have to be found to finance that war without going into debt. Then, undoubtedly that way can be found in order to look after those people who are suffering so terribly.
I do not wish to occupy the time of the house unduly; but for the sake of those who in the future may want to know something about the way in which we did things in these days I should like to put on record, as

an illustration of the suffering which our people are undergoing, a case which has come to my attention. The men who fought and bled and of whom many died for these people, are suffering as this man is suffering to-day. The letter I have in my hand, dated May 31, 1938, is written from Spokane, Washington. I shall quote passages from it, to save time. As a matter of fact, I shall quote from two letters from the same man, one of which was written to me and the other to an official in Alberta. Here are some of his words:
I do not know if you have heard of my misfortune or not, but I have had my right foot amputated. I have had one hearing, and they will give me one more, but I cannot prove that I contracted this Buerger's disease in France. I was in a British hospital in London, but they did not put down all my record, or it has been lost. I was treated for chronic otitis media, trench fever and trench feet. I have suffered ever since I came out of army with my right foot, but did not know what was wrong until last summer. I was to several of the best doctors in Spokane, and they all . said it was Buerger's disease. This disease had been traced back to France. The United States government has a large hospital at Soap Lake near Spokane treating eases like mine, and they are all returned soldiers. Most of these men have had several amputations, and there is no cure for it. This water is used and mud baths stop the disease, but does not cure it. There is no question in the United States government but w h a t, these men got this disease in France, and all draw pensions and hospital treatment. I have sure suffered with this, and still am. My leg is not healed up yet.
Was operated on December 7, 1937. I have never asked for any relief of any kind. Have paid my own bills, but I have been down since I came here three years ago. I moved down here on account of my wife's health. She is not strong. She has had three operations, and she has been working keeping me and my two boys since I came here. But I do not think she will be able to last much longer at the work she has to do.
I wish you would see if you can find any of my records or not. If you cannot see if you can see some of the pensions officers, and maybe you can do something for me. I had Doctor Mulloy treat my foot in 1927 and in 1931, so you can see it has been bothering me for a long time.
Those are some of the quotations. And here are quotations from a letter written by the same man on the same date to an official of the Alberta government. Before I begin reading these passages, I submit they are so pathetic as to be disgraceful to the officials of this dominion. All. we have to do is to put along with what I have read some further things I shall read, to see how pathetic the whole thing really is:
I wrote your Uncle Hugh and received an answer from him, but he could find no record of me. Went to the hospital I was in London

Pension Act Amendment
but all records had been sent to war office. He went to the war office and all Canadian records have been sent to Ottawa. So he could not do me any good.
I have had one hearing in the pension board, and I was turned down on account there was no record of me having anything wrong with my foot. I have suffered ever since I came out of army, but I did not know what was wrong with my foot until last summer, and doctors who examined me told me it was Buerger's disease.
Part of this may be repetition of what I have already read.
But my foot was so far gone they had to amputate it. These doctors I had examine me say I got this in Trance, and I was to some of the best doctors in Spokane.
The next part of the letter is much the same as what I have already read. Then, there is this touching part :
The Red Cross has taken care of me up until now, but don't know what I am going to do now. I know I contracted this _ in France-but try and prove it to those pension men. I don't suppose any of those guys stood in that mud and rain. It is funny any of us fellows have any feet. I stood in mud sixteen days once, and was on duty all that time. Never did have dry feet-and freezing weather.
I know I am sure entitled to some compensation, if any soldier is. I cannot work and my wife is trying to make a living and send our boys to school. She is not very strong. She has had three operations, and I left up there on account of her health. I wish you would do what you can. If you do not think I have suffered with this foot, ask my mother. She knows how long I have been bothered. I went to Doctor Mulloy in 1927 and also in 1931, but he did not know what was wrong.
I was treated a little for trench feet in the hospital, but they have no record. We used to sit with our feet in coal oil. I have seen several of the boys in the ward I was in with toes and parts of their feet just rotting away. I was in a British hospital in England, and I do not think half the records were kept. Three thousand patients in this hospital, so you can see they were busy and maybe some of the records were lost, or not even put on record. Let them read this letter and see if they would like to be a soldier and get the breaks we got.
I am a member of the Canadian legion, and we have a pension office here. And they have helped me and are still working on my case, and all of the legion say I am entitled to it. I have not asked for pension until last fall, and I have paid all my doctors' bills myself and I do not know how much I have paid. I never asked for a cent of relief in my life, yet. But I am down now and cannot work, and I do not suppose I ever will be able to.
Mr. Speaker, I knew that young man when as a boy, blooming, fresh and vigorous at eighteen years of age, he signed up. I knew that boy when he was returned, and when he signed up again. I know his family. They are in my constituency; I know them all by name. I know that what that boy says is
the absolute truth. But can we get anything for him, to help him?-no, sir. I am going to read to the house a letter he received on March 10, 1938. But before doing so, may I say I do not blame the officials in charge. In my judgment they are as fine and sympathetic a lot of men as one could put together. But the laws which we in this parliament have passed have bound those men, with the result that they must write something like what I am going to read:
The commissioners, having reviewed your claim for entitlement to pension in respect of Buerger's disease resulting in amputation of right foot are regretfully of the opinion that this condition has no relation to your service. The commissioners' decision reads as follows:
"This man had two periods of service. He first enlisted February 4. 1915. Served in Canada only and was discharged September 17, 1915, medically unfit.
He reenlisted March 31. 1916, served in France and was discharged November 21, 1917. On his second enlistment he was treated for pyrexia of unknown origin. He was returned to Canada in November, 1917, because of preenlistment defective hearing.
The date of application for Buerger's disease October, 1937. Claim is made that the Buerger's disease originated with the pyrexia of unknown origin on service. First evidence of treatment is that of Doctor Mulloy of Cardston, who states he treated Ellison in 1927, and again in 1931. The evidence fails to show relationship to service, and the application is not granted."
I should like to invite your attention to the printed letter which I am enclosing. This sets out certain information with which you are entitled to be furnished, relative to proceeding further with your application, should you desire to do so.
May I just point out to members of the house that that man was down there, on his back. His wife was working to keep the wolf from the door. They are trying to put two boys through school. And yet he is granted a permit to come up here to Canada to present his case again!
I am going to read the letter which I wrote to the authorities on June 27, 1938. This was addressed to General H. F. McDonald, chairman of the Canadian pension commission, and reads:
There is coming before your commission some time this summer the case of R. D. Ellison. West 2215, Mallon Avenue, Spokane, Washington. U.S., who is requesting pension as a result of Buerger's disease contracted while on service in France which resulted in the amputation of a foot.	,
You will doubtless, I know, appreciate any first hand information to aid you in making your decision. As Mr. Ellison enlisted from my constituency and as 'both be and all his family are personally well known to me, I am perhaps in a position to give you as accurate an account of his past as anyone in Canada.
Before he enlisted he seemed well and strong. His family are all vigorous, healthy people, and the only physical defect which could be in

2312	COMMONS
Pension Act Amendment
any way detected in Mr. Ellison was a slight defect in his hearing. He was particularly impressed upon my mind because of his rather outstanding athletic ability and achievements, and I think we could safely assume that before going to France his limbs were sound.
The fact that he reenlisted seems to me to weigh heavily in his favour as you know that it took plenty of courage and patriotism for a youth. to sign up once; .to sign up a second time after having had experience in that awful struggle required genuine heroism.
Your own observations must have proved to you that many men are of such self-sacrificing, stoical, and independent make-up that they scorn to think of having the state or anybody else keeping them. They enlisted to serve their country and their king and to fight for the cause; especially was that the attitude of our noblest prior to and immediately after 1914. The result was that after discharge many men who were suffering minor pains and disabilities omitted to mention them feeling that they would wear off, or that such disabilities were only to be expected and to be courageously endured by any man whose lot it was to serve in war.
Mr. Ellison and his family generally are of that rather stoical make-up, and the result was that for a long time, although apprehensively aware that all was not right in his feet.^ he did not inform the officials of his condition as he could not know that there might be developing in his limbs a slowly progressing malignant malady such as Buerger's disease. This of course caused him to neglect to keep such evidence as he might have kept tending to prove that his disability was traceable to his hardships in France, where at one time I am informed he stood in mud and rain for sixteen days; a performance sufficient to destroy the health of anyone. It would appear that any man who had gone through such a trial would never again be the same: that his vitality would be permanently impaired, and that the tissues of the parts of his body particularly subjected to such a strain would have their resistance to malady definitely weakened.
In the case of a man who has gone through such rigours, I believe every possible allowance ought to be made to give him the full benefit _ of any doubt. The fact that he is in the United States will not predispose any judge against him when it is remembered that he had to go down into Washington for his wife's health.
Mr. Ellison is in painful need; he is deserving of his country.
I am sure that this man's case received every consideration which could be given to it. This is a letter I received under date of July 2 1938:
In the absence of General McDonald, I have to acknowledge your letter of June 27 last in the above noted case.
On the first hearing of Mr. Ellison's case, the commissioners, with great regret, were unable to find that Buerger's disease had any relation to service, and the application had to be disallowed.
Mr. Ellison, however, has asked that his case proceed to a second hearing and he has appointed the dominion command service bureau of the Canadian legion in Ottawa to represent 
him during the second hearing. Mr. Ellison may rest assured that, if it is at all possible for the commissioners to grant him a pension, they will be only too glad to do so.
I may add, as regards the last paragraph but one of your letter, the fact that Mr. Ellison is living in t'he United States has no bearing whatsoever on his claim. The domicile or nationality of a pensioner or an applicant for pension is immaterial to his claim.
There is nothing wrong with that letter. It is just as kindly, sympathetic and earnest a letter as could be written. I am sure all was done that could be done or that was implied in that letter would be done. Having left at home the next letter which they wrote me, I called up the pensions branch and asked them to send me a copy of the letter they had sent later on dealing with this case. I am putting all these details on the record because I want to be perfectly fair to all the people concerned. I want to bring the case up to date, up to the day on which we are considering it. This is the letter I received from General McDonald under date of March 14, 1939:
I am enclosing herewith copy of a letter which was addressed to you on July 2, last, with regard to Mr. Ellison's case. Since that time Mr. Ellison has been awarded a slight aggravation in respect of otitis media and received a gratuity in this respect for $100 as the disability from this condition is very slight at the present time.
The most serious condition he has is Buerger's disease. The commission have not found that the evidence which has been submitted has been sufficient to relate this condition to his service, but it is now being investigated further by two commissioners who are in the west at the present time, and I have been advised by them that they are seeking advice from the doctors who attended him in the United States at Soap Lake, Washington, and they are making an endeavour to visit that place in order to further consider the matter so that if possible every bit of evidence in Mr. Ellison's favour will be brought out. I do not anticipate that their final decision will be given for a few weeks yet, but I will let you know just as soon as I receive it.
Let me hasten to say that with these letters, with the attitude of these men, with the attitude of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) there is absolutely no fault to find. They are doing everything which lies in their power, and yet this man is suffering as no Canadian who fought for his country should be allowed to suffer. The responsibility rests upon us in this chamber.
I think I have spoken as long as I choose to speak, but there is one thing more I should like to say. In my opinion we are treating our returned men in a niggardly fashion. If Canada were a poor country in which there was not the means of an abundant life, it would be a different matter. But there is in

Pension Act Amendment
this dominion a superabundance of everything that a returned soldier needs to support himself and his family. The fact that we are not making it possible to give to the returned men a sufficiency of that abundance will stand as a condemnation of us and of our generation. How that sufficiency could be given is another matter, but it can be given. Of that there is no possible doubt.
There is just one more observation I believe I shall make before I sit down. Hon. members must have been disturbed by the fact that to-day in the Dominion of Canada and throughout the British empire there is not that fervent alacrity and readiness to serve which existed when we were young men. Why? Largely because of the way in which we are treating these returned men. It is hard enough to-day for a young man to live when he has all his limbs and faculties. Only this summer I spoke to one young man who will be available for the next war. He said that when war comes they would have to go, but he was going to do everything in his power to get into the air force or the navy. When I asked him why, he said the reason was that it would be all over quickly. If we believe we can build an army strong enough to fight the future foes of this land out of men who have been so disheartened that they say things like that, then we are not facing realities. In the very interests of this country and the safety of our empire, such changes should be made as will make the young men. upon whose shoulders the burden of the next war will fall, feel that there is at least some possibility of their being compensated in some measure for the terrible sacrifices which they will be called upon to make. It is my plea, sir, that something be done before it is too late.

speechtext:
I want to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that many cases have been rejected by the board on account of technicalities which I think the minister should take some cognizance of and do his best to remedy. I have in my riding a man who served overseas. Before enlisting, he was an athlete in the pink of condition. At the front he was gassed and shell-shocked. He spent considerable time in hospital, and when he came back to the city of Hamilton he was examined only for his heart, and possibly his dental condition. Within a couple of months of his discharge he became troubled with bronchial and asthmatic conditions. Before his discharge he had been passed as fit by one of the doctors who thought he was doing this chap a good turn. Various doctors stated that his bronchial and asthmatic conditions were the result of his war service, but like a good many other soldiers he fought his battles alone and did not wish to become a burden to the country. Three or four years later, when he was no longer in a position to support himself, his savings and earning capacity having gone, he applied for a pension, and he was told, "Your board states that you were discharged physically fit." But, Mr. Speaker, we can produce doctors who will state that undoubtedly this man's condition was caused by his war service.
Another soldier was awarded a partial disability pension for bronchial trouble. He is now becoming absolutely deaf. Physicians for the board say that his deafness has nothing to do with his bronchial trouble. On the other hand, we have specialists who will state that the deafness was undoubtedly caused by the bronchial and asthmatic conditions for which he was receiving a partial disability pension.
Another case is that of the widow of a soldier who was receiving a pension. Some of the doctors stated that the soldier's death was probably caused by his war service. Other doctors attributed it to something else. I
Pension Act Amendment

think that in such circumstances, where a soldier served overseas for three or four years, was wounded and subjected to gas attacks, he should be given the benefit of any doubt.
Then there is the wife of a returned man, with six children. He was turned down for a pension, and his wife says, "I am going to vote communist in the next election because the government is not looking after the returned men who fought overseas."

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to enter into any monetary discussion of where we are going to find the money to pay for these pensions, as my hon. friend to my left (Mr. Blackmore) started to do, but there are two or three matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister.
I think this bill is a good one. If I understand it correctly, it does away with the appeal board in Ottawa and sets up appeal boards which will come a little closer to the problems which have to be considered. But I wonder if it would not have been better if the bill had gone a step further and set up some kind of sympathetic board such as they have in England. I am sure the minister knows of this board and that some five hundred cases in England, which would have been a travesty on justice if left as they were, were looked after by the board. We have a great many such cases in Canada, border-line cases of one kind or another, such as a chap in my riding who was afflicted with a funny nerve disease called disseminated sclerosis. The minister no doubt knows the name. It strikes you here, there or some other place in the body. I think the minister understands. But it is very difficult to say just what causes this disease. There is a very great difference of opinion between the doctors, whether this disease is a result of war service or not. I endeavoured to get a pension for this man, who had this borderline disease, but his application was turned down. I think if we had some kind of sympathetic board such as they have in England, and they had seen the record of this man and the difficulties he had gone through during the war, he probably would be getting a pension now. But he was turned down flat.
There are a great many of these cases, and it is difficult to know whether their disability at present is the result of war service or not. We do know that some men are better off as a result of the medical attention they have received during their service, but there

are others who seem to go down hill later on, and therefore it is hard to find out whether their trouble is attributable to war service.
To a certain extent I am in favour of this bill, but might it not have been a good idea to extend it a little? There is another class of men, for example, who might have been considered, the imperial veterans. The imperial veteran is like an outcast so far as pensions in Canada are concerned. After all, he is a Canadian and he gets a very small pension from the British government. Living conditions in Canada are different from those in England, and he is having more and more difficulty as time goes on in securing what may be called his rights.
My suggestion to the minister last year was that he should allow these veterans to avail themselves of the services of the advocates connected with our pension department. I do not think the suggestion was too far afield, that the imperials might have the service of the pension department's advocates so that they might be saved expense in their efforts to obtain the pensions which they deserve but apparently cannot get.
There is another point. Last year I was the first member to bring up in the House of Commons the plight of the war widows of Canada. There are not so many of them that should be receiving pensions. We must remember that when our boys went overseas, from 1914 to 1918, they were told that Canada would look after them and their dependents. Canada has done a pretty good job so far, but what do we find now? We find that the war widow whose husband was in receipt of less than eighty per cent pension has great difficulty in getting a pension at all. If her husband dies of a non-pensionable disease, she has a very hard time. If he dies of cancer or of some disease of that soft, she is out of luck, but if he had died two or three days later of a pensionable disease she would get a pension. There are about 2,000 war widows in Canada whose husbands were receiving pensions of from ten to eighty per cent disability, and their maximum pension would be $60 a month. If the husband dies of a non-pensionable disease, the widow is out of luck. But why should she be cut off just because the man dies of a non-pensionable disease whereas, if he lived two or three days longer and died of a pensionable disease, she might have some chance of obtaining a pension?
If these 2,000 war widows obtained $60 a month each, the total would be only about $1,144,000 a year, and that is not very much

Pension Act Amendment
for the country to pay to redeem all the promises made to our soldiers when they went overseas originally, and the assurance given them that their dependents would not want. I think we might easily have gone further in this bill and extended it to cover these war widows. We must also remember that times are getting harder. These women are getting older all the time, and it does seem a pity that they should be destitute, sometimes with children to look after. They helped their husbands when they were getting a thirty or forty per cent pension and we might have done something in their behalf.
There is one other point which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It comes under the Militia Act, but I will bring it up now. In 1919 the Militia Act was revised with respect to pensions. The pensions of those in the militia were increased, but those poor fellows who were pensioned before 1919 have now the same status that they had then. Nothing was done about them. I have asked the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power) whether he could not persuade the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) to do something under the Militia Act to take care of these men. There are only about ninety or one hundred of them in Canada to-day, and I do not think that these injustices should continue.
I am glad to see that the Pension Act is being amended. I believe the quorums will be in closer touch with the cases and we shall consequently have more justice. I do wish the minister would consider setting up what we might call a sympathetic board to adjudicate on these border-line cases that appeal to our sympathy. We are all anxious to see that no injustices continue against those boys who went overseas and gave such service to the country. I could bring down a volume of .pension cases and read them to the house. I have upstairs in my room seven or eight hundred petitions, as one might call them, from war widows. I should be glad to have them bound and give them to the Minister of Pensions for his attention.

speechtext:
I know that one of the
outstanding reasons which make it difficult for a returned man to get a pension is that they were in such a hurry to get home that they signed off. I said to one man, "Why were you in such a hurry to get home?" He said, "Look here, Dan, if you had not seen your wife and two wee kiddies for four years you would break your neck to get home." And I suppose I would. I know this Pension Act has been improved year after year; I know that after examining the files in the pension board I realized that I had been too hasty in forming a conclusion. I have the record of eight returned men and two war widows who, I think, are entitled to pension, and a generous one. I will give the case of one man who was receiving a fair pension. He had many wounds, and was not as fit for work as the average man. Seemingly he was never out of pain; the only time he had any relief was when he got tight. Then one day something happened, he went down into his own cellar and passed out suddenly. His wife cannot get a pension.
I am proud to-day of the attitude of our returned men all over Canada in relation to our empire and the defence of Canada; many of them are ready to offer their services again. I repeat my question to the minister: Will these people, men or women who have not been successful up to the present time, have any hope under this bill of getting a pension? When I came down and told the story and showed the facts concerning one man, he got a pension, and whether it was the excitement or what, he lived only two weeks after that. I could take the chairman of the pension board into a home in Fort William today, and unless there is something very peculiar on the file I am sure that man would receive more consideration.
We are told that returned men should get the benefit of the doubt. I know from my experience in about ten cases that they got the benefit of the doubt. I am sure that the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power) is just as keen as we are to see that every soldier gets his due, and I am sure he will do his best. I have not any fault to find with any official. But I am anxious to know whether there will be any hope for these people under this bill when it is shown that there is an outstanding need.

speechtext:
This bill deals almost wholly with the abolition of the appeal court, and a few minor but some fairly substantial changes, all of them for the benefit, I think, of the returned men.
Pension Act Amendment

The minister must be gratified at the almost unanimous support his bill has received; I have not heard or read any criticism of what is in the bill, but merely of what is not in it, so to speak. I was not in the house when the earlier debate on the second reading took place, but I have read it in Hansard since, and particularly the speeches made by hon. members from British Columbia, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who gave in temperate and non-partisan language a clear exposition of the situation as we see it in British Columbia, where there are so many returned men. Apparently they joined in asking that the minister submit the bill to a pension committee to be set up as in former years. I should like to join in that request. We think of the committees in the past, of which the minister himself was always the most prominent member and very often the chairman, and of the great work he always did in that regard. That was one committee, I think about the only one, that deliberated in a non-partisan spirit, and its report, which was generally unanimous, was of such a character that the government could readily give attention to it, being distinguished, I repeat, by the absence of any political element.
Sending this bill to such a committee would enable a number of matters to be debated, some of which have been touched on here to-night, which it would be impossible thoroughly to discuss here, because the officials are not here and the minister cannot reply to questions until we go into committee; in any event, there are many phases which cannot be adequately discussed in committee of the whole house. I received a letter this morning-I have it before me now; I did not know this question was coming up tonight-touching on a number of features, all of which have been put before the house by Dne or another of the hon. members from British Columbia. The question of pensions for veterans of the Fenian raid could also be debated before that committee. Even in a political sense I cannot see that the government would have anything to lose by setting up this committee and referring the bill to it, with these other questions which have come up. For one thing it would save a great deal of time and relieve the government of responsibility. The report would probably be unanimous, as I think it always has been; the government could say in defence of their action before the country that this nonpartisan committee agreed to so and so,

whereas if they go ahead as they are doing now they will have to accept the whole responsibility for matters for which they are perhaps not entirely responsible. Therefore I should like to join with the other hon. members who have urged that pensions matters go to a committee.
It appears probable from the program outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-day that we are going to be here for a long time yet, and there will probably be ample time for such a committee to sit and consider the whole question; and after all the government have control of both the committee and the house. It would give the ex-soldiers and their representatives the feeling that they got a run for their money at any rate, and that their grievances have received consideration. Some are sound and fundamental, others quite casual and perhaps not deserving of great consideration, but in any event they will be discussed without partisan bias by soldiers; for most of the committee would be ex-soldiers, representing every section of the house and the country. That would be to the benefit of the government and of the country, and certainly it would give the soldiers a feeling of satisfaction even if they did not get all they seek; they would have the satisfaction at any rate of knowing that their case had been heard fairly and fully by an unbiased tribunal.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I
deem it my duty to take part in the debate on the second reading of Bill No. 6, the purpose of which is to amend the Pension Act. I was a member of the committee which was set up by the house to study the problems of returned men in 1936. The meetings of the committee in that year were interesting to me, and a great deal of progress was made towards the solution of some of the problems confronting the returned men. Since 1936, however, no meetings of that committee have been held, and I believe the time has now come when the committee should sit again to take into consideration the problems which have arisen during the last two years.
The bill now under consideration provides for two changes. The first is the abolition of the pension appeal court and the setting up of appeal boards of the commission, each consisting of three members, in place of the present quorum of the commission. The second change simply extends the time for pension applications to the year 1942.
I am not so much concerned as to whether or not this is a wise move. I am more concerned with the result than with the methods

Pension Act Amendment
adopted to obtain that result. This change in the act is simply a change of method; we are changing from a pension appeal court to an appeal board of the commission. As I have just said, I am more concerned about the results which we shall obtain from that change than with the methods to be followed. If the results are no better than those of the past, then I must condemn the change. If, on the other hand, we have the word of the minister that it is for the good of the returned soldier, that it will be more beneficial to him, then I am heartily behind the minister. In reference to the second change, the extension of the time to 1942, this simply means that returned men who saw service in an actual theatre of war may have until that year to make application for pension; in other woi'ds, it extends the time to one year beyond the life of the present parliament.
I believe the success or failure of the new set-up will depend entirely upon the attitude of mind which will be brought by the members of these boards to the consideration of the cases that come before them. If they concentrate their attention more upon the financial aspect than upon the moral aspect of ^the situation, then no good will result. If, on the other hand, they are genuinely sincere in desiring to find a solution to the problems of the returned men, the change will be indeed worth while. In advocating that the committee should sit during this session, however, I do so because other problems concerning the returned men require attention. These problems have been outlined already by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), but perhaps I may be pardoned if I list some of them again. No provision is made in any of the acts-I do not use the word "pension" because that is a method of bringing about a certain result-for children born after May 1, 1933. No provision is made in respect of the wife of a pensioner married after May 1, 1933. No provision has been made to take care of the widow of a pensioner unless he dies of a pensionable disability or was in receipt of a pension of eighty per cent or more. These are very important problems which should be discussed by the committee this session. I feel quite sure that the committee, working harmoniously as it did in 1936, could bring in recommendations that would be adopted unanimously by this house.
There is one other problem that has not been tackled as yet; that is the submission that the remainder of the returned soldiers unemployed be provided for by the payment
of an allowance to be known as the provisional economic allowance. I believe that is something which should be carefully studied as a possible method of bringing about a certain result, and I believe that committee, if it were called together and given an opportunity of discussing this important matter, could arrive at something that would be well worth while. So I would add my voice to those who have already spoken, in asking the minister in all sincerity to cal! the committee together during the present session in order that we may discuss some ot the important problems that confront the returned men at the present time.
