speechtext:
There are just one or two observations I should like to make, Mr. Speaker; and without taking time to reiterate what has been said by some of the other hon. members who have spoken, let me tell the minister that I endorse the first half of the remarks made by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) in regard to the cases he cited. I endorse what was said by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) in regard to war widows, and also what was said by the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Brown). With regard to the last half of the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge, in connection with finding the money, I disagree with him.
I should like to make this other observation, which I made in this house three years ago. It will not be very long before most of these cases are taken care of by Father Time. Another decade will see a large rfumber of these men pass on. So could not this House of Commons, as a unit, support any legislation that will see to it that we as a body do our bit until such time as these men are removed from the scene by time? In that connection I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the plight of the widows, as mentioned by the hon. member for St. Paul's. If a census were taken to ascertain the number of widows who are not in receipt of pensions, and the number of widowers who served overseas and who are not receiving pensions, I think it would be found that there were twice as many widows as widowers.
My point is that a medical man in giving his findings might say that a soldier [DOT] had probably died from cancer. Perhaps the minister will agree that cancer is one of the diseases which carries off a great many returned men. It may be that their illness from that disease is not related to war service. The same individual might have been shell-shocked and subsequently discharged from the army as being fit. Then, a number of men who served overseas might pass away from heart
Pension Act Amendment

attack, which could not be attributable to war service. Nevertheless these men have left widows and dependents behind them.
Since their return from overseas the men who had families to provide for found themselves competing with another generation which had grown up during the time they were serving overseas. The returned men have found it difficult to compete in the labour market and to earn sufficient to provide themselves even with the bare necessities of life. Some of those men have passed away, leaving their families more or less destitute through no fault of their own.
My observations are not a reflection on the conduct of the department over which the minister has the privilege of presiding. I believe that ever since the war the department under very difficult circumstances has been trying to do a job. On most of the occasions it has been my privilege to pass judgment on the department I have found fair treatment. I believe the minister will agree with me that only rarely have I found it necessary to speak to him. In fact, since he has been minister of the department, I do not think he has seen me in his office many times.
Coupled with these remarks I should like to make this further one, that I do not believe in any other constituency in Canada there are more cases for consideration by the pension branch than in the one in the suburban area outside Toronto it has been my privilege to represent. I have found the men concerned quite reasonable in their requests. On the other hand, I have found the department and the pension commission reasonable and considerate in the discussion of cases.
But what I want to urge at this time is this: As the time is very short, let us all as a unit, including all parties, do everything humanly possible for the returned men and widows, so that generations to come will be able to say that in this particular regard we have not failed.
I am sorry that I could not follow that section of the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge in which he set out his method of finding the money which would be required. I believe the hon. member outlined the Social Credit method of finding the money. As an alternative, may I suggest a more practical way of doing it? It would appear that in the next two-or perhaps six months, depending upon the temper of the house-staggering sums of money will be voted. In those sums I do not include moneys required by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). I would hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) would find ways and

means for an equal distribution, or a distribution having regard to the principle of representation by population. I should like to see the ministry rise in its place-and by the way I see my point has not been clearly understood by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). I was suggesting that instead of the Minister of Public Works trying to figure out supplementary estimates amounting to many millions of dollars to be distributed according to the principle of representation by population, otherwise known as "rep. by pop," that you, sir, as Minister of Mines and Resources and as one of the senior members of the cabinet, together with other ministers of the crown, just take that public works money which we shall be asked to vote, cut it in half, and give the remaining half to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) for purposes of pensions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I did not intend to speak to-night, but I rise for the purpose of complimenting the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) upon bringing down this revamped legislation. I believe it is a step in the right direction; it is an expression of
what is in the heart of every hon. member. We all want to see something more done for the returned man if it is at all possible.
In fairness to those who were not old enough to go overseas, but who were quite near that age, let me say that they too should receive some consideration from this government and from hon. gentlemen irrespective of party. Hon. gentlemen opposite spoke of these returned men as those who are going down the lane where there will be a last turn before they eventually go to mother earth.
I think we should remember that this parliament has been very generous in its desire to do the best it possibly can for these men.
I do not want to minimize the service of those who went overseas; I do not want to minimize the service of those who remained at home worrying and wondering whether their loved ones would return-there are those who sacrificed their lives and have asked nothing in return for the great sacrifice they made.
I rise only for the purpose of saying that we should not get the returned soldier in a frame of mind where he thinks that very little has been done for him. Every hon. gentleman knows that in connection with the appointment to every civil service position there is a thirty per cent benefit in favour of the returned soldier. If a return could be made of the positions in every department of government, it would show the large percentage of overseas men who have been appointed to the service and who are now receiving their earthly reward for their fine soldierly service. I do not want for one moment to minimize the service that anyone gave in the great war, because that came very close to me. I saw my young nephew off on a transport which left Halifax, but to-day he is buried in Prance. He died when only eighteen years of age. Like many others he gave his life for what Woodrow Wilson said was to make democracy safe for the world.
Camp Hill hospital is located in my constituency, and I am glad to see that the minister is making it possible for greater help to be given to the .returned soldier who is not able to work because of his overseas service. As I understand this legislation, these men will now be permitted to enter hospital for treatment. Previously they were turned away. I know of returned men in Halifax who are ill, who are nervous, who are suffering many pains, but who have not been permitted to enter the hospital for treatment. The staff in the hospital receive large salaries and are almost falling over each other in
Pension Act Amendment

carrying out their medical and surgical duties, but these men cannot get treatment. I am not talking about the man who is able to go about and enjoy God's sunlight and fresh air; I am talking about the poor returned soldier who is ill, but to whom these doctors have previously turned a deaf ear. I am glad the minister has provided for the hospitalization of these men.
By this legislation these applications may be reopened until 1942. These are comprehensive measures. I heard some hon. member across the floor say that the estimates of the Department of Public Works should be cut in half, one-half being handed over to the returned soldiers. The Department of Public Works, under the able management of the deputy minister, Mr. Hunter, and the chief engineer, Mr. Cameron, see to the needs of Canada in connection with breakwaters, wharves, dredging and various other matters which are important to the whole of Canada. They must be looked after because, if Canada dies, how can we look after the returned soldier?
These are just a few passing thoughts which came to my mind as I listened to the hon. gentlemen speak. I think there is the desire on the part of all hon. members, irrespective of party or group, to do the best possible for the returned man and to pass such^ enabling legislation as will be comprehensive to all, whether or not he be learned in the law. For these reasons I am proud to congratulate the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health, and if in his judgment and the judgment of the house the bill should go to a special committee, there to be gone over and made more straight and less devious for the returned soldier and his widow and dependent children, I shall be pleased on all occasions to give the best that is in me to bring about such results and to make the returned soldier and his dependents feel that we have not forgotten those who fell in Flanders fields where the poppies grow.

First, I want to say that I think everybody is convinced that in the minister hijnself the department is headed by one who for years has held a very prominent place in this house in the battle for the rights of the returned soldiers; and under him the minister has in General McDonald one for whom the returned men have every respect and the warmest regard.
I heard a member say a few moments ago that he had more returned men in his riding than in any other, but I doubt if any riding has more returned men than the riding of 
Toronto-Davenport, in which is situated Earlscourt, from which so many, many regiments went overseas.
I have read the bill through just casually, and I may have overlooked something that I had in mind, namely, the hope that the bill would contain some easier provision applying to the widows of returned soldiers. I have several such cases in mind, but I do not think it is necessary for me to mention them specifically at the moment. There is, however, one in particular that has been under my notice for some time, the claim of Mrs. Fuller, whose husband died in the north country, through having been frozen to death on his way back to civilization. I hope that if this bill is referred to a special committee, as I understand is the minister's intention, provision will be made for hearing the widows of returned soldiers, so that they may appear and present their cases in connection with amendments that may be proposed to take care of this class.
I have nothing further to add, but as one representing many returned soldiers I do hope that the sad lot of so many of them who have not received consideration, will be improved through the provisions of this bill.
^ Mr. N. J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): Mr. Speaker, before this bill receives its second reading, I want to associate myself with those who have spoken on behalf of the ex-service men.
Reference has been made to the fast declining number of ex-service men, and that is all too evident throughout Canada. There are one or two classes that I should like particularly to mention. I am heartily in accord with giving all the support that can be granted to the widow of the returned soldier. I know the minister knows, as does every member of this house, that there are a great many widows of returned soldiers who have nursed their husbands through long sickness. The soldier may have been in receipt of a partial or total disability pension, granted sometimes upon compassionate grounds, through the benefit of the doubt being given where the particulars on the discharge certificate were not too clear. Then, when the soldier has died, technicalities are raised, possibly a postmortem is held, and the benefit of the doubt is not given to the widow and family of the deceased soldier, although to the average lay mind it would seem that the widow and the family should be provided for through a pension.
I know of such cases. One returned soldier was receiving a considerable pension. He died and his widow has now two sons growing up to manhood. Through a technicality these

Pension Act Amendment
two sons have the humiliating experience of seeing their mother being forced to go out to do domestic work, and it is difficult for these boys who are growing up to understand why the pension of their father, who gave his all for this country, is not permitted to be carried on for at least a few more years to his widow until perhaps she reaches the time when, she would be eligible for old age pension.
These are tragic cases, and surely when this bill is under consideration in committee some consideration will be given to providing for them. More latitude should be allowed. We know that the officers of the several departments are most efficient. Tribute has already been paid to them and it does not need repetition at this moment; nevertheless the officials repeatedly say: "We have to live within the terms of the act." I say, Mr. Speaker, let us try to make this act a little more in keeping with our humanitarian ideas, and so I trust that the minister in his wisdom and the committee in their deliberations on this bill will be able to enlarge its provisions to take a little better care of just such cases as I have mentioned. These two boys, who are now growing up to manhood, have seen their father's life sacrificed, his pension cut off, and his widow forced to go out to work simply because his discharge certificate did not contain all the information it should have contained.
Widows and their growing families, descendants of our war veterans, are being robbed of their rights just because some little detail was neglected. I appeal for greater consideration for these soldiers' widows and their families, so that there will not be a blot on the records of this parliament in our treatment of the families of the men who were promised so much when they went overseas in 1914, and so that the growing sons of our returned men, if we should within the next few weeks face similar difficulties again, will not in bitterness say, "If I go I expect to get the same treatment my father got." It is up to this government to see that there is no possible recurrence of these cases. It is up to us in this parliament and it is up to the people of Canada to keep faith with the veterans who went overseas, many of whom are still suffering anguish and all kinds of hardships. Let us keep faith with them and show that Canada stands behind the men who stood for us in our time of need.

speechtext:
This section is the only one which does not deal with the wiping out of the appeal court. But it does deal with the so-called dead-line. This section should receive the careful consideration of all hon. members. As I understand it, there was no dead-line for applications for pension before the sitting of this parliament in 1936. At that session, the first one of this parliament, a deadline was imposed in this way: First, all men who served only in England or Canada were cut off as of the first day of July, 1936. After that date no veteran in either one of those
two groups could apply for pension. A soldier who served in a theatre of war was given until January 1, 1940, to apply for pension. After that date he would have to get special leave from the pension commission before he could even apply. There was considerable argument about that provision in 1936 before the special committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems. Many of us felt that there should be no dead-line for the veterans who had served in France. To-day I am more convinced than ever that that dead-line should be wiped out, that no' such obstacle to obtaining a pension should be placed in the way of our fighting men who saw service in a theatre of war. I ask this committee to-night, regardless of party-because, after all, these soldier problems are not party matters-to do away with this dead-line. This section of the bill merely proposes to push the dead-line ahead two years, to January 1, 1942. Before that time it will have to come up for consideration again. I submit that there should be no dead-line for the fighting men. Those who apply for pension now, have to trace their disability right back to the time of the war, a very difficult task in itself, without having to get over another hurdle of getting permission from the pension commission even to apply. Many of our returned men who were wTounded, who actually bear wounds received overseas, are not drawdng pension because, although wounded, they have not broken down. As time goes on and these men get older, they break down as a result of their wounds. Men of that class should not be handicapped when they come to the pension commission to get compensation for disability.
In May, 1936, the house provided for a degree of finality in these matters by providing for the first time that, on what is called second hearing, an applicant had to claim for every disability. There was no such thing as coming back again in a year or two and asking compensation for some additional disability; he had to put all his eggs in the one basket. Also, the number of pension applications has been dropping year by year. In the fiscal year 1937-38, it dropped by 646 as compared with the previous year, and there had been a drop in each year for several years. So, for these reasons too, I suggest to-night that we wipe out this dead-line. For that purpose I move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), which I think will accomplish that end:
That bill No. 6, to amend the Pensions Act, be amended by substituting for section 8 thereof the following:
Pension Act Amendment

8. Section 12A of the said act, as enacted by section 11 of chapter 44 of the statutes of 1936, is amended by repealing all but the first line thereof and substituting for the portion repealed the following:
"who did not serve in a theatre of actual war shall not be awarded unless application therefor has been made before the first day of July, 1936."
If this amendment is passed, section 12A will read: "a pension for disability of a member of the forces who did not serve in a theatre of actual war shall not be awarded unless application therefor has been made before the first day of July, 1936." In other words, it leaves the dead-line as it stands at the present time for the man who served only in England or Canada, but completely wipes out any reference to a dead-line for the veteran who served in a theatre of war. I believe it is only just that there should be no dead-line for those men who, after all, were Canada's fighting men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I have some doubt as to whether this amendment is quite in order. However, I pass that over for the moment.
I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the fact that from the time pensions were commenced, until 1930, there was always a dead-line, beyond which date applications would not be received. As a matter of fact, I think when the committee met in 1928 the dead-line had been passed, and there was a period of six or eight months during which applications for pensions could not be legally received. No great harm was done, however, there was a renewal of the dead-line, and that had been done every year or every two years. In 1936 this question was given a great deal of consideration by the committee. If the deliberations of that committee should have any authority in this house, this was one of the matters most fully discussed, namely whether or not it would be possible to set a dead-line for applications for pension. As my hon. friend has said, a dead-line was established for applications from people who saw service only in Canada. In 1936, with the unanimous consent of the committee, provision was made in the legislation under which a man, even if he were barred by the time limit, could still come before the commission and have his case considered. As a matter of fact, I think it was the unanimous opinion of the committee in 1936 that the only purpose served by a dead-line was to prevent frivolous claims from being entertained; that anyone who had a real, substantial claim could be heard under the act.
This year I came to the conclusion that there was no agitation on the part of returned soldiers, their associations or anybody else,

to have this dead-line extended; but after some consideration, just in case there might be some injustice done, I thought perhaps I had better ask parliament to extend the period for another two years. But even that date is not a dead-line, in that the returned soldier has every opportunity to have his case heard and considered even after 1942, the date established in this bill. I believe the principle is good. As the house knows, in Great Britain the dead-line was set at seven years after the war. If we make certain, by legislation which was unanimously approved by members of the 1936 committee, that no injustice will be done, I hardly think my hon. friend's point is well taken.

speechtext:
I submit there is ample justification for the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I well remember the discussion in the committee, and my understanding was that the matter was temporarily left in abeyance. The argument of the minister that the dead-line was established by previous parliamentary committees, and that therefore a dead-line should be set now, I suggest is hardly well founded. The reason the dead-line has been advanced from time to time by parliamentary committees is that it has been shown there are still men who have the right to establish entitlement under the act. There are many men who for various reasons have not advanced their claims. They may have been in prosperous circumstances and, out of some feeling of independence, felt that they should not go through the procedure required to establish entitlement. Now, perhaps on account of advancing years or depressed economic conditions, they are seized with the importance of establishing entitlement, particularly having regard to their dependents.
I am particularly interested in the ex-service men who dwell in remote settlements. I have had some experience in visiting the homes of ex-service men living in small settlements up the Pacific coast, and have been astonished at their ignorance with regard to their rights under the act. There are many men who to all appearances could easily establish entitlement to pension in respect of disabilities resulting from wounds; they bear the marks of the wounds on their bodies, but they have not the slightest idea of their rights under the act, and have not advanced their claims. The

Pension Act Amendment
difference between the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver South and the method suggested by the minister is that under the amendment these men will have the right to advance their claims for entitlement to pension. The minister's proposal leaves it purely as a matter of discretion with the pension commission. We have no quarrel with the commission to-day; but there may be changes in the personnel; various things may occur, and those in charge of the administration of this act at some future time may not view matters in the same way. I suggest that it should always be clear that a man who served in a theatre of actual war can establish that he is suffering from a disability incurred during service, and there should be no statutory limit as to the date of application. As a matter of right, he should be able to advance his claim to entitlement; and I suggest that the very fact that from time to time we have found it necessary to set this date forward is ample justification for eliminating from the act any dead-line at all, thus leaving that right clear and unmistakable.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
With regard to the amendment which is before the committee, I would quote Beauchesne at page 165, citation 555:
No increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
I also quote from Bourinot, at page 407:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer. On one occasion, in the English commons the consent of the crown was given to certain formal resolutions proposed by a private member with reference to charges in courts of law to be defrayed out of the consolidated fund. It was thought, however, that any resolution placing a charge on the consolidated fund should be moved by a minister of the crown, and the more regular procedure was thereupon carried out. It was distinctly affirmed, however, that the member who proposed the motion involving the charge was within his right when he had the sanction of the crown, but it was generally admitted at the same time that it was better, as a matter of policy, that the proposition should emanate from a responsible adviser of the sovereign.
I therefore rule this amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
move the following amendment:
That Bill No. 6 be amended by substituting for .the year 1942 where it appears in section 8 thereof the year 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Order.
It is the same point, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I have the same objection
as I had to the other amendment. I believe the committee ought to understand that what is being done under the amendment the government is proposing is to allow an applicant to make application until 1942. Under the present Pension Act he is precluded from making application after 1940. We propose extending the time for two years. In his amendment the hon. member for St. Paul's wishes to extend it for twelve years. I would suggest to the committee that sufficient unto the day is the good thereof. It is only an argument on the question of quantum.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
We are not moving the
amendment just to be funny.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It looks like it.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
There are many cases in British Columbia of fighting men who have been wounded and who realize that sooner or later they will have to apply for pensions. The great majority of them have no idea whatsoever that there is such a thing as a dead-line. If this bill were passed, after 1941 those men would have to apply to a pension commission in Ottawa to get leave to apply for pension. If the pension commissioners at
Pension Act Amendment

that time happened to be hard-boiled, or if at that time there happened to be a depression, then it would probably be just too bad for those veterans.
I would point out that about 75,000 Canadian veterans who were wounded on service are not yet drawing pensions. They are the men who are going to be faced with this hurdle. Why make a farce of it? The minister has said that a dead-line was imposed before and that it was lifted; that it was imposed and lifted again, and so on. Why not cut out the dead-line and stop 'fooling with the question? Let those fighting men know that if they can prove in 1945 or 1948 or 1950 that they are disabled because of something that happened in the war, they will receive their pensions, without having to jump over the additional hurdle of getting from the pension commission a permit to apply for a pension.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: If a man is going to be entitled to a pension to-day, to-morrow, five, ten or twenty years from now, then he is in fact entitled to that pension. I do not not see any reason why there should be any dead-line. Then, if the dead-line is placed at 1942, we shall be placing a handicap on the man who thinks he may have something wrong with him in the following years. He will be hustling, and thinking up some excuse to get in under the wire. A man either is or is not entitled to a pension. There is no reason in the world why he should be precluded from getting it. The amendment suggests that it should be extended to the year 1952, which would give some further time.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I do not see why the hon. member should be so much worried about the dead-line. Apparently on former occasions it has been changed, and I think if in 1942 it is believed that there are still men who are entitled to pension but who have not been able to avail themselves of the opportunity to apply, we can still revise the dead-line, and make it expire two or three years farther on.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Why should we have to revive it for two or three years? Why not leave it open?

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I think the question has been well explained by the minister. A committee. considered this matter and they thought it desirable to have a dead-line. As I have said, it would be an easy matter to extend the date; that has been done before.

speechtext: Apparently under this revised section 21 the new appeal boards will not have the power to grant a compassionate allowance, whereas previously the court of appeal had that right. subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

I do not think we shall be
depriving anyone of much opportunity because the appeal court granted only three all the time it was functioning. I am hoping the appeal board will be more generous. The appeal board is really the Canadian pension commission sitting in appeal, so it will be made up of practically the same people.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: The inferior court, that is the pension commission with two commissioners, has the power under this section to grant a compassionate allowance, and yet the government is setting up a superior court with three members of the commission, a court which actually sees the man but which has no power to grant such an allowance. That does not seem reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister explain under what circumstances a widow or dependent child is entitled to a pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: At the present time a widow of any soldier who dies as a result of his war service is entitled to a pension, if married prior to January 1, 1930. Since the war, 11,000 pensioners have died, and 6,000 widows are now in receipt of a pension. In order to be absolutely sure that the benefit of the doubt would be given to the widow of a soldier, it was enacted many years ago and continued in 1936 that if a man were in receipt of an eighty per cent pension, or over, that is, was in classes 1 to 5, no matter from what disability he might die his widow would be entitled to a pension. Perhaps this would be as good a time as any to state that before this bill finally passes, I propose to proceed to introduce legislation whereby the widow of a man who was in receipt of a pension of fifty per cent or more will be entitled to a pension, if married prior to January 1, 1930. I want to make it clear to the committee that this will not meet the current agitation of the widows by any means, and it is not intended that it should. The current agitation is to permit the granting of a pension to the widows of all ex-soldiers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Will it be retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: If a man were in receipt of a pension of fifty per cent or more and died ten years ago, his widow would be entitled to a pension but not to ten years' back pension.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Fifty per cent or more?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Classes to 1 to 11.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: How many will that take care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Not very many. It will take care of four or five hundred, which is a small number compared with those who are now pressing the government to have their claims attended to. That is why I want to make it clear that it is not intended to meet that agitation in any way, shape or form. But it is intended to give assurance that the widow of a soldier who was in receipt of a fifty per cent pension or more will get the benefit of the doubt. I think it will give the benefit of the doubt in so far as it is possible to give it. If we were to go below that, it would no longer be a question of giving the benefit of the doubt, it would be a question of giving a pension on purely sympathetic grounds. If we stop at fifty per cent, I think hon. members can be assured that the country is endeavouring in so far as it can to give a pension to the widows of those who have died as a result of their war service.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It is now eighty per cent and over?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It is now eighty per cent and over; we are coming down to fifty per cent. The mechanics of working that out will perhaps be somewhat complicated. I suppose I shall have to proceed by way of resolution to move an amendment to the act. It will simply be an amendment to section 32, subsection 2, to change the words from "one to five" to "one to eleven." Should the house approve the resolution and the amendment, I shall endeavour to consolidate it with the present bill before it is sent to another house.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister consider removing the restriction on children born after May 1, 1933?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I hardly think so. The
expense of that would be something like $850,000 annually.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: To provide for children who were born after May 1, 1933?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I have gone into that quite thoroughly, and I find that we would be taking on something like 17,000 children, even assuming that the fecundity rate would be
Pension Act Amendment

lower on account of the increasing age of our soldiers. The best figure I can get is 17,000 children bom since 1933.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: That makes it all the more unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It did make it all the more unfair when they were cut off in 1933.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I wonder if under section 10 the commissioners would have discretionary power in dealing with the widow of a pensioner who was married after 1930. In this case it was a one hundred per cent pension. It is the case of a much married man, who was married in 1902 and deserted his wife and was divorced in 1907. In 1909 he married No. 2. He deserted her in 1917 while he was overseas. Two years before he was pensioned he married No. 3, representing himself as a single man. In 1922, No. 2 turned up, and he acknowledged her as his legal wife, although he continued to live with No. 3. Hon. members laugh, but it is not so very funny. It is a most unfortunate case. By No. 3 there was a child born, and the man in acknowledging No. 2 as his legal wife did assign a portion of his pension to her, although in the interval before she turned up, No. 3 had been receiving a portion of that pension. But after No. 2 came to light again, No. 3 was required to refund that portion which she had received. No. 2 died in April, 1931, and immediately after, No. 3 was again legally married.
Here is a case where No. 3 had lived with that man as his acknowledged wife, had married innocently, lived with him for twenty years and had a daughter by him, and it does seem that the lapse of a very short period made the situation most unfortunate. The man died last year, and the widow of course received no pension whatever. I would ask the minister if he would not give consideration to bringing in an amendment to cover such a case, putting the line at 1931 or 1932. That would remedy this case, which certainly seems to be a deserving one because it is quite apparent that this woman did not marry the man for the sake of the pension. He had represented himself as a single man, and after living with him for twenty years I think she deserves a pension, but because she was not legally married to this man until after January, 1930, she gets no pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps that is a case that might be looked after under the meritorious clause, section 21.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Can the minister give us an idea as to how many wives would be affected by removing the line now set at May 1, 1933? He said there were 17,000 children.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: We estimate about 2,400 wives, but it is only an estimate, and even the number of children is only an estimate. It is based on the fact that in the twelve months prior to May 1, 1933, there were 4,041 children born to pensioners and placed on pension; in the next twelve months 4,655, and so on, and with an annual reduction of ten per cent for loss of fecundity to which I referred, we come to the figure of about 17,000 who would receive the additional allowance. The cost would be $850,000.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I think that is a pretty high estimate.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I understand that there are about 2,000 pensioners' widows at the present time who are not receiving pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Probably, yes.

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: But is not the principle the same as with a pensioner? The pensioner is entitled to ten or twenty or thirty per cent or any other percentage. It is not a gratuity which is given by the Dominion of Canada, but something to which the pensioner is entitled by law. Now the minister is proposing to draw the dead-line at fifty per cent. I cannot see any reason for such a discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Does the hon. member want me to withdraw my proposal?

subtopic: ABOLITION OP PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I would suggest that these widows, whether the pension be ten per cent or any other per cent-and ten per cent does not amount to anything-are entitled to the pension just as much as the pensioner is entitled to his.
